extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, practitioners, and examiners handling PCT (international) applications
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing and complying with the PCT 'unity of invention' requirement (PCT Rule 13), including what constitutes a single general inventive concept, how unity is tested, procedural consequences of lack of unity, and response/protest options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of invention basic requirement (PCT Rule 13)
rubrics_metrics.description: An international application 'shall relate to one invention only or to a group of inventions so linked as to form a "single general inventive concept"' (PCT Rule 13).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the overarching mandatory requirement for PCT filings: all claimed subject matter in the international application must either be a single invention or a set of inventions that are linked by a single general inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test for unity — special technical feature
rubrics_metrics.description: The requirement of unity is fulfilled only when there is a technical relationship among the inventions involving one or more of the same or corresponding 'special technical features'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'special technical feature' is one that defines a contribution which each of the claimed inventions makes over the prior art. Each claimed invention in the group must share such a feature (or corresponding features) that provides a common contribution over the prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of lack of unity: a priori vs a posteriori
rubrics_metrics.description: Lack of unity may be 'a priori' (apparent before considering the prior art) or 'a posteriori' (becoming apparent only after considering the prior art, e.g., the purported shared feature turns out to be known).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners may object to unity on either basis; applicants should be aware that an apparent common feature can be negated by the prior art discovered in search, converting an a priori unity into an a posteriori lack of unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: ISA entitlements when unity lacking (consequences)
rubrics_metrics.description: If unity is not met, the International Searching Authority (ISA) is entitled to request the applicant to pay an additional search fee for each invention beyond the first or to limit the international search to the invention first mentioned in the claims if no additional fee is paid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants faced with a lack-of-unity finding can either pay additional search fees to obtain searches on further inventions or accept a limited international search. The ISA's actions are procedural consequences that affect the scope of the international search report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Response options and protest procedure after additional fees
rubrics_metrics.description: After payment of additional search fees the applicant may file a protest consisting of a reasoned statement explaining why unity is met or why additional fees are excessive, pay a protest fee, and have the matter reviewed by a review body; if the protest is justified, partial or total reimbursement may be ordered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The protest procedure is the formal recourse against ISA unity findings and/or fee demands: it requires a reasoned argument, payment of the protest fee, and may result in reimbursement. Applicants should prepare reasoned statements addressing the special technical feature and contributions over prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common categories of claims presumed to satisfy unity (PCT heuristics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under PCT certain combinations are commonly presumed to satisfy unity: product + process for making it + apparatus for making + use of product; multiple products that share a 'special technical feature'; combinations where there are corresponding contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When drafting claims, coupling product, its making process, apparatus, and uses, or ensuring multiple products share a defined special technical feature, helps avoid unity objections. These are practical drafting heuristics rather than strict rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differences between PCT unity and US restriction practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The PCT unity standard is 'single general inventive concept' (special technical feature) with mechanism of additional search fees and protest recourse, whereas US restriction practice (35 U.S.C. 121) uses 'independent and distinct' + 'serious burden' standards with election among groups and petition recourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should not assume US restriction outcomes map to PCT practice: mechanisms, standards, and remedies differ. For US-bound PCT filings, plan strategy knowing the PCT applies its unity standard in the national stage rather than the US restriction standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic considerations for claim drafting and prosecution
rubrics_metrics.description: Plan claim structure to minimize unity objections (especially for US-bound PCT applications), consider whether to prosecute multiple inventions abroad in the same case, and remember that US national stage applications use the PCT unity standard, not US restriction standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical strategies include drafting claims to emphasize a shared special technical feature, deciding whether to pursue separate filings in key jurisdictions, and anticipating additional search fees or protests. Use the 'common categories' heuristics and be mindful of differences in national practices.
